mainTopic: How far a renter may use the outside of a large building; when resting a beam on a neighbor's wall becomes a חזקה; and אביי's rule about roof fences for two houses facing each other across a רשות הרבים
overview: The amud opens at the end of a ruling about what a renter in a large building may use: its walls and projections, but not the front garden. רב נחמן in his own name and then רבא each widen this, first to the front garden and then to the back yard. רבינא teaches when a beam resting on a neighbor's wall becomes a חזקה: after 30 days, after 7 days for a סוכה, and right away if it is set in clay. אביי rules that two houses facing each other across a רשות הרבים must each fence half a roof. The גמרא explains why the public street matters and why the rule is not obvious. Next, שמואל requires a four-אמות fence between a roof and a neighbor's courtyard, while רב נחמן requires only a ten-טפחים partition. The גמרא explains that this partition marks a theft boundary and defends it against a ברייתא. רב הונא and רב חסדא then argue about who builds the wall between courtyards at different heights, and a ברייתא supports רב חסדא. The amud ends with a story of a collapsed lower floor whose owner asks the upstairs neighbor to rebuild. The ruling comes on the next amud.

steps.title: What a renter may use in a large building
steps.stepSummary: The ruling ends by saying that a renter in a large building may use the projections and walls up to four אמות, and the wall's thickness where that is the custom. He may not use the building's front garden.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a large building, the renter may use its projections and its walls up to four אמות. He may use the thickness of the wall where that is the local custom. But he may not use the building's front garden.
steps.whatsHappening: We are coming in at the end of a ruling, given just before this, that רב נחמן reported in his teacher's name. It lists which outside parts of a big building a renter may use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter gets the building's outer projections and walls, but only up to four אמות from his own space. Using the thickness of the wall depends on local custom. The front garden is left out completely.

keyTerms.meaning: A large building with many apartments
Projections or ledges that stick out from a wall
The thickness of the wall
The front garden or courtyard in front of a palace-like building
In a place where this is the custom

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a brand-new statement. It is the second half of a ruling that started just before this part of the daf. The person who "may use" these things is the renter.

phrases.english: In a large building,
he may use its projections and its walls
up to four cubits,
phrases.notes: Measured from the renter's own room outward.

phrases.english: and the thickness of the wall, in a place where they are accustomed to do so;
but the front garden of the building — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ruling that began just before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A renter in a large building may use the projections and walls up to four אמות, and the wall's thickness where customary, but not the front garden.

steps.title: רב נחמן in his own name allows the front garden
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, speaking for himself this time, lets the renter use even the front garden. He still does not allow the yard behind the houses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן himself said: the renter may use even the front garden. But the open yard behind the houses, he may not use.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן now gives his own opinion, which is more generous than the ruling he reported before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The front garden, which the earlier ruling did not allow, is now allowed. A new limit is set further out: the back yard is still off-limits.

keyTerms.meaning: His own, meaning in his own name and not quoting someone else
The open yard behind the houses

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman himself said:
phrases.notes: "Himself" means this is his own view, unlike the ruling just before, which he was passing on from his teacher.

phrases.english: even the front garden of the building,
but the yard that is behind the houses — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the earlier ruling by also allowing the front garden
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The renter may use even the front garden, but not the back yard.

steps.title: רבא allows even the back yard
steps.stepSummary: רבא goes furthest and lets the renter use even the yard behind the houses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the renter may use even the yard behind the houses.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the most generous opinion and allows the one area that רב נחמן had still forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each opinion goes one step further out from the renter's room: walls, then front garden, then back yard. For רבא, even the back yard is included in what the renter may use.

keyTerms.meaning: Even; used to push a ruling one step further

steps.whatToRemember: Three levels: the first ruling allows walls and projections but not the front garden. רב נחמן allows the front garden but not the back yard. רבא allows even the back yard.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
even the yard that is behind the houses.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ רְחָבָה שֶׁאֲחוֹרֵי הַבָּתִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens רב נחמן's view to include the back yard
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The renter may use even the yard behind the houses.

steps.title: A shade beam on a neighbor's wall becomes a right after thirty days
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rules that if someone rests a beam for a shade-covering on his neighbor's wall, it is not a חזקה during the first 30 days. After 30 days it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: a beam for a shade-covering resting on a neighbor's wall is not a חזקה for up to thirty days. After thirty days, it is a חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new ruling about using a neighbor's wall. רבינא teaches when a beam placed on it becomes a lasting right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the neighbor stays quiet for less than 30 days, his silence proves nothing; he could say he thought it was temporary. Once 30 days pass without a protest, the beam's owner has a חזקה to keep it there.

keyTerms.meaning: A beam
A covering made to give shade
An established right to keep using something, gained by use without protest
Thirty days

phrases.english: Ravina said:
This beam for a shade-covering,
phrases.notes: He means a beam resting on the neighbor's wall.

phrases.aramaic: עַד תְּלָתִין יוֹמִין – לָא הָוֵי חֲזָקָה,
phrases.english: up to thirty days, it is not an established right;
after thirty days, it is an established right.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ruling, also about using another person's wall
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A shade beam on a neighbor's wall becomes a חזקה only after 30 days without protest.

steps.title: A סוכה beam takes seven days, and a beam set in clay is a right at once
steps.stepSummary: רבינא adds two cases. For a סוכה built for the מצוה, the beam becomes a חזקה after 7 days. If the beam was attached with clay, it is a חזקה right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is a סוכה for the מצוה, it is not a חזקה for up to seven days, but after seven days it is. And if he attached the beam with clay, it is a חזקה immediately.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא continues his ruling with two cases that change the 30-day timeline.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During the seven days of סוכות, the neighbor can say he kept quiet because it was obviously just for the holiday. If he still says nothing after the seven days, it counts as a חזקה. Fixing the beam in with clay looks permanent from the start, so not protesting right away already counts.

keyTerms.meaning: A סוכה built for the holiday מצוה
Clay or mud used to fix something in place
Immediately

steps.whatToRemember: The time needed for a beam to become a חזקה depends on how temporary it looks: 30 days for shade, 7 days for a סוכה, and right away if it is set in clay.

phrases.english: And if it is a sukkah for the מצוה,

phrases.aramaic: עַד שִׁבְעָה יוֹמִין – לָא הָוֵי חֲזָקָה,
phrases.english: up to seven days, it is not an established right;
after seven days, it is an established right.
And if he attached it with clay,
immediately it is an established right.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds special cases to רבינא's 30-day rule
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סוכה beam becomes a חזקה after 7 days; a beam fixed with clay becomes a חזקה immediately.

steps.title: Two houses across a public area each fence half a roof
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules that when two houses face each other across a רשות הרבים, each owner builds a roof fence on half his roof. The two fences must not be opposite each other, and each one goes a little past the halfway point.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: if two houses stand on two sides of a רשות הרבים, each owner makes a מעקה for half his roof. The fences are not opposite each other, and each adds a bit extra.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a new rule about neighbors protecting each other's privacy on their roofs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each owner fences a different half. Together the two fences block the view between the roofs, and neither neighbor has to fence his whole roof. Each fence goes a little past the middle so there is no gap to see through.

keyTerms.meaning: A public area, such as a street
A fence or railing around a roof
Opposite, facing
Adds a little extra, beyond the halfway mark

phrases.english: Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנֵי בָתִּים בִּשְׁנֵי צִדֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים –
phrases.english: Two houses on two sides of a public domain:
this one makes a fence for half his roof,
and that one makes a fence for half his roof,
this one not opposite that one;
and he adds a little extra.
phrases.notes: Each fence goes slightly past the middle of the roof, so no gap is left to see through.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: שְׁנֵי בָתִּים בִּשְׁנֵי צִדֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ruling about privacy between neighbors
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each neighbor fences half his roof, on opposite halves, each a little past the middle.

steps.title: Why mention a public area at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why אביי spoke about a רשות הרבים. The same rule should apply if the space between the houses were private.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why specifically a רשות הרבים? The same should be true even with a רשות היחיד between them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of אביי's ruling. It asks why he picked a public area when the rule seems to fit any case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes that every detail in a ruling teaches something. If the rule works just as well with private land between the houses, the words "public domain" seem extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Why specifically? A question asking why a detail was mentioned
A private area

phrases.english: Why specifically a public domain?
Even a private domain too!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions a detail in אביי's ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: The words "public domain" in אביי's ruling
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule seems to apply to private land too, so mentioning a public area looks unnecessary.

steps.title: A public area was needed to block a possible excuse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that אביי needed to mention a רשות הרבים. Otherwise one might think a neighbor could say, "You have to hide from the public anyway."
steps.simpleTranslation: He needed to mention a רשות הרבים. Otherwise you might have said that one neighbor can tell the other: in the end, you need to hide from the people in the public area anyway.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by explaining what mistake we might have made without the words "public domain." The next step finishes the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a public street between them, one neighbor could argue: since you must already protect yourself from everyone on the street, fence your whole roof yourself and leave me alone. אביי mentioned a רשות הרבים to show that this argument does not work and the half-and-half rule still applies.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary for him to say
You might have said; introduces a mistaken thought the ruling comes to prevent
In the end, anyway
To hide oneself, to keep private

steps.confusionAlert: The neighbor's argument here ("you have to hide from the public anyway") is the mistaken idea, not the הלכה. אביי's ruling comes to reject it.

phrases.english: A public domain was necessary for him,
lest you say: let him say to him:
phrases.notes: One neighbor is talking to the other here.

phrases.english: In the end, you need
to hide yourself from the people of the public domain;

steps.triggerLanguage: רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים אִיצְטְרִיכָא לֵיהּ – מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about why a רשות הרבים was mentioned
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why a detail was needed ("you might have thought")
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With a public street in between, a neighbor could refuse to help, because the other must hide from the public anyway.
steps.terutzMaskana: אביי mentioned a רשות הרבים to show that this excuse is rejected. Step 9 gives the neighbor's reply that defeats it.

steps.title: Why a neighbor's view is worse than the public's
steps.stepSummary: The neighbor can answer that the public sees him only some of the time, but the neighbor across the way sees him all the time.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי teaches us that the neighbor can reply: 'The public sees me by day but not at night. You see me day and night. Also, the public sees me when I stand but not when I sit. You see me either way. And the public sees me only when they make an effort to look. You see me without even trying.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer from Step 8. It explains why a neighbor cannot say, 'You already have to hide from the public anyway.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being seen by the public is limited: only by day, only while standing, and only when someone bothers to look up. A neighbor sees you all the time and without any effort. So the neighbor's view is a new and bigger harm, and he must still share in building the fence.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us (the point of the ruling is...)
The public, people passing in the street
They look carefully, they make an effort to look
By itself, without even trying

steps.whatToRemember: Being seen by your neighbor is a much greater invasion of privacy than being seen by the public. So 'You can be seen from the street anyway' is no excuse.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that היזק ראיה is measured by how often and how easily someone can see you, not just by whether you can be seen at all.

phrases.english: It teaches us that he can say to him:
The public sees me during the day,
but at night they do not see me;

phrases.aramaic: אַתְּ – בֵּין בִּימָמָא בֵּין בְּלֵילְיָא חָזֵית לִי.
phrases.english: you see me both during the day and at night.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, רַבִּים – כִּי קָאֵימְנָא חָזוּ לִי,
phrases.english: Alternatively: the public sees me when I am standing,
but when I am sitting they do not see me;

phrases.aramaic: אַתְּ חָזֵית לִי בֵּין כִּי קָאֵימְנָא בֵּין כִּי יָתֵיבְנָא.
phrases.english: you see me both when I am standing and when I am sitting.
The public sees me when they look carefully,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לָא מְעַיְּינוּ לָא חָזוּ לִי;
phrases.english: when they do not look carefully, they do not see me;
you see me even without trying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the תירוץ of Step 8 by giving the neighbor's reply to the הוה אמינא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the ruling had to mention רשות הרבים: to teach that the public's view does not cancel the neighbor's duty.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the neighbor could say, 'You have to hide from the public anyway, so my view adds nothing.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The neighbor's view is constant and effortless, unlike the public's, so each neighbor must still build his share of the fence.

steps.title: Isn't the half-roof fence rule obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes אביי's rule about each neighbor fencing half his roof and asks why it needed to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master (אביי) said: 'This one builds a fence on half his roof, and that one builds a fence on half his roof. The fences are not opposite each other, and each one goes a little past the middle.' But isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to אביי's ruling from Step 6. It challenges it as too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both neighbors cause the privacy problem, it seems plain that each should fix his half. So the גמרא asks what new point אביי was teaching. This sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A fence or railing on a roof
And he adds a little extra (past the halfway point)
It is obvious! (Why say it?)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר: זֶה עוֹשֶׂה מַעֲקֶה לַחֲצִי גַגּוֹ,
phrases.english: The Master said: This one makes a fence for half his roof,
phrases.notes: "The Master" here is אביי, quoted from Step 6.

phrases.english: and that one makes a fence for half his roof,
one not opposite the other, and he adds a little extra.
It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to אביי's ruling in Step 6 to ask a new question about it.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's ruling that each neighbor fences half his roof.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Splitting the work equally seems obvious, so the ruling seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: When one neighbor already built his half
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed when one neighbor built first: the other cannot pay him to build the whole fence, because the builder can say his own walls would be strained too.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed when one of them went ahead and built his half. You might think the other could say: 'Take money for the cost, and you build the whole fence.' So אביי teaches that the builder can answer: 'Why don't you want to build? Because it would weaken your walls. My walls would be weakened too!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. אביי's rule teaches something in the case where one neighbor already built his half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once one neighbor has built his half, the other might try to pay him to finish the whole job, so his own roof stays untouched. The builder can refuse. Extra building would put weight on his walls too, so each must build on his own roof.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case
You might have said (the mistaken thought)
The cost, the expense
A wall or foundation
Gets weakened or damaged

steps.whatToRemember: Each neighbor must build his own half of the fence on his own roof. One neighbor cannot push the whole job onto the other by offering money.

phrases.aramaic: לָא צְרִיכָא, דִּקְדֵים חַד מִנַּיְיהוּ וַעֲבַד.
phrases.english: No, it is needed where one of them went ahead and built.
You might have said that the other can say to him:
Take the cost and build all of it yourself;
It teaches us that he can say to him:
You, why do you not build?
Because your wall would be weakened;
my wall too would be weakened.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דִּקְדֵים חַד מִנַּיְיהוּ וַעֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ruling to a specific case (לא צריכא) where its point is not obvious.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: After one neighbor builds his half, the other could pay him to build the whole fence.
steps.terutzMaskana: The builder can refuse, since extra weight would harm his walls just as much. Each builds half on his own roof.

steps.title: A roof next to a neighbor's courtyard needs a four-אמות fence
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quoting שמואל: a roof next to a neighbor's חצר needs a fence four אמות high. Between two roofs, no fence is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: A roof next to his neighbor's courtyard needs a fence four אמות high. But between one roof and another roof, no fence is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about privacy, this time between a roof and a neighbor's courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A courtyard is used all the time, so looking into it is a serious invasion of privacy. That is why the fence must be very tall, four אמות. A roof is not used regularly, so no fence is needed between two roofs.

keyTerms.meaning: Roof
His neighbor's courtyard
Four cubits, a height taller than a person

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
A roof next to his neighbor's courtyard:

phrases.aramaic: עוֹשֶׂה לוֹ מַעֲקֶה גָּבוֹהַּ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת.
phrases.english: he makes for it a fence four cubits high.
But between roof and roof, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new privacy ruling, moving from facing roofs to a roof next to a courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A roof next to a neighbor's courtyard needs a four-אמות fence. Between two roofs, no fence is required.

steps.title: רב נחמן's own view: ten טפחים is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן himself disagrees: no four-אמות fence is needed, only a partition ten טפחים high.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן himself said: He does not need a fence four אמות high, but he does need a partition ten טפחים high.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives his own opinion, which differs from what he quoted from שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל wants a fence tall enough to fully block the view. רב נחמן requires only a ten-טפחים partition. It does not fully block the view, but it is still a real barrier.

keyTerms.meaning: His own (opinion)
He is not required
A partition ten handbreadths (טפחים) high

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the units. Four אמות is about the height of a tall person, but ten means ten טפחים (handbreadths), which is much lower.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל requires a fence four אמות high next to a neighbor's courtyard. רב נחמן requires only a ten-טפחים partition.

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman himself said:
He is not required to have four cubits,
but he is required to have a partition of ten.
phrases.notes: "Ten" here means ten handbreadths, not ten cubits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second opinion on the same case as Step 12, lowering the required height.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A roof next to a neighbor's courtyard needs only a ten-טפחים partition, not a four-אמות fence.

steps.title: What is the ten-טפחים partition for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests רב נחמן's ten-טפחים partition against three possible purposes, and none of them seems to fit.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it for? If it is to stop the damage of being seen, we need four אמות. If it is to catch him as a thief, a simple fence of pegs is enough. If it is for young goats and lambs, a fence just high enough that they can't leap over is enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן: a ten-טפחים partition seems to be the wrong size for every reason we could give for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each purpose calls for a different height. Privacy needs four אמות, which is more than ten טפחים. Marking a boundary against theft, or keeping animals from jumping across, needs less. So ten טפחים looks too short for one purpose and too tall for the others.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage caused by being seen; loss of privacy
Being caught as a thief; crossing over will clearly count as stealing
A low, simple fence made of pegs or stakes
To leap across headfirst in one jump

phrases.english: For what?
phrases.notes: He is asking what רב נחמן's ten-טפחים partition (step 13) is for.

phrases.english: If it is for the damage of seeing,
we need four cubits!
If it is so he can be caught as a thief,
a mere fence of pegs is enough!
If it is for young goats and lambs,

phrases.aramaic: בִּכְדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִזְדַּקֵּר בְּבַת רֹאשׁ סַגִּי!
phrases.english: enough so that they cannot leap across in one jump is sufficient!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the ten-טפחים partition that רב נחמן just required.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's requirement of a ten-טפחים partition
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every possible purpose calls for a height other than ten טפחים, so that number seems arbitrary.

steps.title: The partition removes the excuse of a trespasser
steps.stepSummary: The partition is for catching a thief. A peg fence is not enough, because a trespasser can claim he was just stretching. Nobody can make that claim about a ten-טפחים wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really it is so he can be caught as a thief. With a peg fence he can slip out of it by saying, 'I was just stretching.' With a ten-טפחים partition he cannot slip out of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the purpose is to catch a thief, and only a ten-טפחים wall does that properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A low peg fence can be crossed by accident or with an innocent excuse. A ten-טפחים wall must be climbed on purpose, so anyone found on the other side has no excuse. That is why the height is exactly ten טפחים, not less and not four אמות.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, in truth; it introduces the answer that keeps one of the options
Slips out of it; dodges with an excuse
A partition ten טפחים high

steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן's ten-טפחים partition is not for privacy. It makes any crossing clearly deliberate, like theft.

phrases.english: Really, it is so he can be caught as a thief.
With a peg fence, he can slip out of it,
[saying: I was just stretching myself],
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the words in square brackets; they come from the corrected wording.

phrases.aramaic: בִּמְחִיצַת עֲשָׂרָה – לָא מָצֵי מִשְׁתְּמִיט לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: with a ten-handbreadth partition, he cannot slip out of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14 by keeping the theft option and explaining why ten טפחים is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifies the purpose and shows why the specific measure fits it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For a theft boundary, any small marker would be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: A small marker leaves room for an excuse. Ten טפחים removes the excuse, so it is the proper height.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to require no fence at all
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if one person's courtyard is higher than his neighbor's roof, the court does not get involved. That sounds like no fence at all, which goes against רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him from a ברייתא: if his courtyard was higher than his neighbor's roof, the court does not get involved. Doesn't that mean no fence is needed at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רב נחמן's ten-טפחים rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes a courtyard next to a roof and says nothing needs to be done. Read simply, that means no partition of any size. That would contradict רב נחמן, who requires at least ten טפחים.

keyTerms.meaning: The court does not get involved; he is not obligated
What, does it not mean...? It proposes a reading of the source

phrases.english: They challenged him:
If his courtyard was higher
than his neighbor's roof,
the court does not get involved with him.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו אֵין נִזְקָקִין לוֹ כְּלָל?
phrases.english: What, does it not mean they do not get involved with him at all?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: אִם הָיָה חֲצֵרוֹ לְמַעְלָה מִגַּגּוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the purpose of the partition is settled, the גמרא challenges רב נחמן from a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא appears to free a person from building any partition at all next to a neighbor's roof.

steps.title: Only the four-אמות fence is not required
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא only means that no four-אמות fence is required. A ten-טפחים partition is still needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. They do not get involved about four אמות, but they do get involved about a ten-טפחים partition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the ברייתא more narrowly, so it fits רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Not obligated' refers only to the tall privacy fence of four אמות. The smaller ten-טפחים partition against theft still applies, just as רב נחמן said.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits; the full-height privacy fence

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'אין נזקקין' as 'nothing at all'. Here it means only that the four-אמות fence is not required.

phrases.english: No;
they do not get involved about four cubits,
but they do get involved about a ten-handbreadth partition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by narrowing what the ברייתא is excluding.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the meaning of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means no partition of any kind is needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only removes the four-אמות requirement. The ten-טפחים partition remains.

steps.title: רב הונא: each owner builds from his own level
steps.stepSummary: Two courtyards are at different heights. רב הונא says each owner builds the wall starting from his own ground level and up.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: about two courtyards, one higher than the other, רב הונא said: the lower one builds from his level upward, and the upper one builds from his level upward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: who pays for the wall between two courtyards that are at different heights.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב הונא, the bottom part of the wall, below the upper courtyard's ground, is only the lower owner's job. Each owner starts sharing only from his own ground level and up.

keyTerms.meaning: The lower one (the owner of the lower courtyard)
The upper one (the owner of the higher courtyard)
From his own level and upward

phrases.english: It was stated:
Two courtyards, one higher than the other:
Rav Huna said:
The lower one builds from his level and up,
and the upper one builds from his level and up.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: שְׁתֵּי חֲצֵרוֹת זוֹ לְמַעְלָה מִזּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new related case about neighbors' walls.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each owner builds from his own ground level upward, so the lower owner alone builds the bottom part.

steps.title: רב חסדא: the upper owner helps from the bottom
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא disagrees. The upper owner must help build the wall starting from the very bottom.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: the upper one helps from below and builds.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives the opposing view: the upper owner shares in building the whole wall, including the lowest part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two argue about the bottom section, which faces only the lower courtyard. רב הונא puts it on the lower owner alone. רב חסדא makes the upper owner share in it too.

keyTerms.meaning: Helps from below; shares in building the bottom part

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
The upper one helps from below and builds.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: עֶלְיוֹן מְסַיֵּיעַ מִלְּמַטָּה וּבוֹנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opinion that disagrees with רב הונא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The upper owner shares in building the wall from the bottom.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the upper owner may not limit himself to building from his own level. He must help from below, as רב חסדא said. It adds that a courtyard higher than a neighbor's roof is not obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with רב חסדא: about two courtyards, one higher than the other, the upper one may not say, 'I will build from my level and up.' Rather, he helps from below and builds. And if his courtyard was higher than his neighbor's roof, he is not obligated toward him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that clearly matches רב חסדא's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא rejects in so many words the claim of building only 'from my level and up', which is רב הונא's position. It ends with the same line quoted in step 16 about a courtyard above a neighbor's roof.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with him
He is not obligated toward him

steps.whatToRemember: Between courtyards at different heights, the ברייתא sides with רב חסדא: the upper owner shares in the wall from the bottom.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the source of the line the גמרא used in step 16. That line belongs to this ברייתא about courtyards at different heights.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita in line with Rav Ḥisda:
Two courtyards, one higher than the other:
the upper one may not say:
"I will build from my level and up,"
rather, he helps from below and builds.
And if his courtyard was higher

phrases.aramaic: מִגַּגּוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ – אֵינוֹ זָקוּק לוֹ.
phrases.english: than his neighbor's roof, he is not obligated toward him.
phrases.notes: This is the same line the גמרא quoted in step 16 to challenge רב נחמן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב חסדא's side of the disagreement from steps 18 and 19.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's view that the upper owner helps build from below
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating that the upper owner may not say 'I will build from my level and up'

steps.title: The lower floor collapses and its owner asks for help rebuilding
steps.stepSummary: Two people live in one building, one upstairs and one downstairs. The lower floor collapses, and the lower owner asks the upper owner to rebuild it together.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two people living in one building. One lived upstairs and one lived downstairs. The downstairs part collapsed. The downstairs owner said to the upstairs owner: 'Come, let us rebuild it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is telling a new story to set up a new legal question. Here it lays out the facts and the lower owner's request.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic, still about neighbors sharing building costs. The lower floor is the base that holds up the upper floor, so the lower owner wants both of them to take it down and rebuild together. The גמרא has not given a ruling yet. It is setting the stage.

keyTerms.meaning: The upper one (the person living upstairs)
The lower one (the person living downstairs)
Broke, collapsed
Were living, were dwelling
Let us build it

phrases.english: There were these two people who were living in one building,
one was living upstairs
and one was living downstairs.
The lower story collapsed.
phrases.notes: Literally 'broke.' It was sinking and no longer good to live in, but the upper floor was still standing.

phrases.english: The lower owner said to the upper owner:
"Come and let us rebuild it."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about a shared building after the discussion of walls between courtyards at different heights.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This sets out the case: the lower floor collapsed and its owner asks the upper owner to rebuild together.

steps.title: The upper owner refuses because he is living comfortably
steps.stepSummary: The upper owner answers that he is living just fine and does not want to rebuild.
steps.simpleTranslation: The upstairs owner said to him: 'I am living just fine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The upper owner turns down the request. Now both sides of the argument are on the table, and the גמרא is getting ready for the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper owner's point is that his own home is still usable, so he sees no reason to tear it down or pay for rebuilding. This sets up a real conflict between the two neighbors. The ruling on who is right comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Well, nicely, fine
I am living (I dwell)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the final ruling. It is only the upper owner's claim. Do not assume the גמרא agrees with him yet.

phrases.english: The upper owner said to him:
"I am living just fine."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אֲנָא שַׁפִּיר קָא דָּאֵירְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the upper owner's reply to the lower owner's request from step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The upper owner refuses to rebuild because his own home is still fine to live in.
